text:
Happy Friday! We're ending a mild day in the 60s, but sunset comes at 4:35 under mostly cloudy skies, so don't count on much color. Tonight stays cloudy and mostly quiet with a low around 44, and a stray bit of drizzle is possible.

Saturday is where the weather turns. A compact storm system swings in from the west, bringing a cooler, grayer day with a high near 53. You may see some light rain in the morning, but it becomes more likely by early afternoon and turns steadier through the evening. The heaviest rain falls late Saturday night into the early hours of Sunday, with a low near 36. If you have outdoor errands, a walk, or yard work, do them before lunch.

Sunday starts damp, with leftover rain through the morning and maybe a few wet flakes mixed in before 1. After that it's mostly cloudy, drier for a while, and brisk out of the northwest. NWS has a high near 51, but the models range from the upper 40s to the mid 50s. I'd lean cooler, upper 40s to near 50, so wear a real coat. Showers return after 7 Sunday night, with a low near 38.

Rain totals for the weekend should land around a third to a half inch, mostly Saturday night. More showers arrive Monday and the week stays chilly, so get the umbrella out of the closet.

AFD DISCUSSION (the forecaster's full reasoning, same regional caveat; their temps are area-wide ranges):
KEY MESSAGE 1: The forecast challenge this weekend is evolution of closed mid/upper lvl cyclonic circulation and track of sfc low pres and associated pops and qpf placement. Sfc analysis shows stationary boundary draped along the Eastern Seaboard with axis of showers and embedded thunderstorms. Meanwhile, GOES-19 water vapor imagery shows a potent/compact closed cyclonic circulation over the central Great Lakes this aftn with north side deformation/moisture over the northern Lakes. This circulation is progged to move southeast toward the Southern Tier of NY by 00z Sunday, while north side deformation and mid lvl moisture axis lifting from southwest to northeast acrs our cwa on Sat aftn. The mid/upper lvl circulation tries to capture sfc low pres by late Sat into Sunday with weak inverted sfc trof developing acrs our cwa. The combination of weak sfc convergence and mid lvl deformation on north/northwest side of closed 850-700mb cyclonic circulation supports high categorical (85-100%) Sat aft into Sunday acrs most of our cwa. As 1000mb sfc low pres lifts acrs eastern Maine on Sunday brisk/northwest upslope flow develops under modest low level caa. It should be noted the airmass behind this system is only marginally cool enough to support summit lvls snow, given progged 850mb temps near 0C and 925mb of 1C to 3C. Any snow accumulations wl be above 3000 ft and generally a dusting to 1 inch, maybe 1 to 3 inches above 4000 ft acrs the High Peaks in Essex County, NY. Rainfall amounts will be 0.30" to 0.60" with localized higher amounts possible in favorable upslope areas of the northern Dacks and central/northern Greens. This general idea of higher pops and qpf is supported by the latest AI-GFS/AI-ECWMF 12z/06z runs respectively. Much cooler temps wl be expected this weekend, especially on Sunday with brisk northwest winds/damp conditions and highs only in the 40s. Next potent s/w energy in the progressive northwest flow aloft arrives on Monday with additional widespread precip likely, especially favorable upslope areas. Progged thickness values are cooler for this system, along with progged 850mb temps btwn -1C and - 3C, supporting slightly lower snow levels. However, still some uncertainty on amount of moisture in nw flow aloft with pw values in the 0.30 and 0.40 range and limited pocket of mid lvl moisture. For now have kept close to NBM pops/qpf and thermal profiles, but expect changes to occur as it becomes a near term forecast focus. Highs Monday wl range from the mid 30s to upper 40s acrs our region. KEY MESSAGE 2: The large scale cyclonic gyre over the Hudson Bay will continue to eject several shortwaves through mid to late next week. Tuesday and Wednesday will see shower chances focused in the higher terrain, with perhaps some blocking against the Greens pushing moisture into the Champlain Valley either day.
